inspect:2611.07859.question: In the controlled closed-search evaluations, how does CORE compare with the Tongyi DeepResearch and OpenResearcher harnesses on answer accuracy, evidence recall, context length, and cost? Which ablations isolate snippet selection, context expansion, and duplicate suppression?

passages.text: Deep research agents answer complex questions through repeated search. They rely on a harness that runs their tool calls and returns evidence to their context. This creates a trade-off: Search works best over long passages, which give enough context for reliable semantic matching. But the returned evidence should be short, because every observation stays in the agent’s context for the rest of the trajectory. We introduce CORE , a training-free harness that combines coarse-to-fine search with context management. CORE retrieves passages with a dense retriever. It then reuses the token-level similarities from a late-interaction reranker to return only the most relevant snippet from each passage. Context management lets the agent expand the context around sources it has already retrieved and suppresses repeated snippets. In controlled closed-search comparisons with the Tongyi DeepResearch and OpenResearcher harnesses, CORE achieves state-of-the-art answer accuracy and evidence recall across three agent models and three benchmarks (BrowseComp-Plus, BrowseComp-Wikipedia and BrowseComp-Plus CM ), on corpora containing up to 553M documents.

The key idea of our CORE, a co arse-to-fine deep re search harness, is to shift this burden from the agent to the search itself: relevant text is found by searching over broad passages, while the agent receives only concise snippets. We organize the search space into documents, passages, segments, and snippets, and treat evidence as the text admitted into the agent’s context to serve the local goal of a sub-query or the global goal of the question. CORE’s search tool first performs coarse retrieval of passages with a reasoning-aware dense retriever ( Chen et al., 2026b ) , then fine-grained reranking with a late-interaction model ( Khattab and Zaharia, 2020 ; Chaffin, 2025 ) , whose token-level similarities also locate the most relevant snippet within each passage at no additional encoding cost. CORE’s context manager lets the agent expand the context around previously retrieved sources and deduplicates snippets across searches. Our contributions are as follows: • Coarse-to-fine search. CORE searches at the passage level but returns evidence at the snippet level. It reuses the token-level similarities computed during late-interaction reranking to locate the most relevant snippet in each passage, without any additional encoding. • A training-free harness. CORE combines coarse-to-fine search with context management and works with any agent model without retraining. Context management offsets the narrowness of snippet-level evidence by letting the agent expand the context around previously retrieved sources, and it suppresses snippets repeated across searches.

• State-of-the-art closed-search results at scale. Under controlled settings, we compare CORE with two recent state-of-the-art open-source harnesses, Tongyi DeepResearch ( Tongyi DeepResearch Team et al., 2025 ) and OpenResearcher ( Li et al., 2026b ) , on BrowseComp-Plus ( Chen et al., 2026c ) , BrowseComp-Wikipedia ( Yang et al., 2026 ) , and BrowseComp-Plus CM ( Sharifymoghaddam et al., 2026 ) . To ensure reproducibility, we restrict the study to closed search over fixed corpora. Across three agent models, CORE achieves the highest accuracy and evidence recall in every model–benchmark comparison, setting new state-of-the-art results to the best of our knowledge.

Table 1: Main comparison results. Answer accuracy and evidence recall are in percent. Peak context is the median, over questions, of the maximum context length in tokens. Tokens/search is the mean number of tokens returned per search call, summed over all subqueries. Search calls is the mean number of search calls per question. Token counts are comparable only within the same agent model. Arrows show the preferred direction, and bold marks the best value in each of these columns within each model–benchmark group. We find that Tongyi-DeepResearch-30B-A3B, using the original Tongyi DeepResearch harness with document-level retrieval based on AgentIR-4B, achieves 63.13% on BrowseComp-Plus, which is lower than the 65.66% achieved by our current passage-level retrieval setup. On BrowseComp-Plus, Jiang et al. (2026) report an evidence recall of 38.1% for Tongyi-DeepResearch-30B-A3B, whereas their Harness-1 (20B) reported the evidence recall at 58.4%.

We presented CORE , a training-free deep research harness that combines coarse-to-fine search with context management. CORE retrieves whole passages to judge relevance, then reuses the reranker’s token-level similarities to return only the most relevant snippet from each one. Context management lets the agent expand the context around sources it has already retrieved and suppresses repeated snippets. Across three agent models and three benchmarks, CORE achieves higher answer accuracy and evidence recall than Tongyi DeepResearch and OpenResearcher in every model–benchmark comparison, while returning substantially fewer tokens per search than Tongyi DeepResearch. These results show that deep research agents can answer more accurately from shorter search responses when relevant text is selected before it enters their context.

inspect:2610.20857.question: How does IDEA2PRIOR evaluate paper-retrieval quality against its baselines, including query selection, relevance judgments, Hit@5 accounting, and retrieval cost? Which components are usable in a handwritten research-digest harness?

passages.text: Finding a paper from an informal research idea requires more than matching topic words: relevant work may use different terminology, and its distinguishing mechanism may be absent from the abstract. We present Idea2Prior, an auditable literature-search system built on PaperArena. It combines multi-source discovery, identity verification, facet-based abstract assessment, semantic citation expansion, and joint Expert ranking. A retrieval-only mode ranks up to five papers from a shortlist of at most 60, using complete available abstracts and locally selected PDF evidence from five fixed acquisition attempts, without generating a long-form report. In a historical comparison covering ten queries from each of EASY, MEDIUM, and HARD, aggregate reported Hit@5 is 53.3% for Idea2Prior, 43.3% for ChatGPT web Deep Research, and 36.7% for Gemini web Deep Research under the documented accounting convention. The advantage is concentrated in EASY and MEDIUM; ChatGPT leads on HARD. Selected Idea2Prior runs average 8 minutes 53 seconds, compared with user-reported web averages of 5.2 and 4.7 minutes. A separate nine-query API sample averages $0.0945 per task; this is a historical cost observation, not a matched comparison with web subscription costs. Pairwise Top 5 coverage ranges from 6% to 34%, showing differing returned evidence sets. The system also exposes optional implementation analysis and citation-evolution tools. These results support targeted idea-to-paper retrieval while leaving general web research, forum search, and broader relevance evaluation open.

Researchers often remember an idea before they remember a title: a neighborhood with uncertain boundaries, a circuit transformation with a particular constraint, or an assistant that recognizes when a complex task changes. Recovering relevant prior work from such descriptions is difficult because vocabulary, application setting, and the level of technical detail can differ substantially between a query and a paper. A useful assistant must retrieve candidates, establish their bibliographic identities, and distinguish a close conceptual match from work that merely shares a topic. LLM-based research systems provide useful ways to explore and synthesize sources. STORM organizes research into multi-perspective information gathering and article outlining [ 3 ] , Co-STORM supports interactive exploration [ 4 ] , and Agent Laboratory connects literature review with experimentation and reporting [ 5 ] . Our focus is narrower: given an idea, which five identifiable papers are most likely to match it, and what evidence explains their selection? This objective is not equivalent to the quality of a general research report. We introduce Idea2Prior, an extension of PaperArena and its implementation [ 1 , 2 ] . The contribution is an engineering and evaluation framework for inspectable idea-to-paper retrieval: it preserves search queries, candidate identities, assessments, filtering reasons, PDF availability, and the final ranking. This makes it possible to distinguish a discovery miss from a candidate that was retrieved but lost during filtering, or from a task that failed operationally. A high-level result alone cannot make those distinctions.

The central design separates inexpensive assessment of a broad candidate pool from a bounded examination of document evidence. After abstract assessment and citation expansion, an Expert model jointly considers up to 60 candidates. Five papers are selected for PDF acquisition; unavailable PDFs are not replaced by additional papers in retrieval-only mode. Complete available abstracts remain in the Expert input, along with evidence availability and up to six locally selected PDF passages per acquired paper. A missing PDF does not make a paper irrelevant and does not prevent it from ranking first. The optional full-report mode retains downstream synthesis for users who need a written literature analysis. The revised evaluation covers 30 query cases: ten from each of three prompt tiers, with shared targets across tiers. The reported aggregate Hit@5 is 16/30 for Idea2Prior, 13/30 for ChatGPT web Deep Research, and 11/30 for Gemini web Deep Research. The ChatGPT total includes one convention-based credit, disclosed in Section 5.1 . Idea2Prior leads both baselines by 20 percentage points on EASY and MEDIUM, but trails ChatGPT by 10 points on HARD. Mean selected-run latency is 8.89 minutes, and a separately reported nine-query cost sample averages $0.0945. Thus the present evidence shows a recovery advantage in two tiers and a low observed API cost, with longer latency than the supplied browser averages. Our contributions are: 1. An auditable retrieval-and-ranking workflow with identity-aware candidate records, semantic citation filtering, and a joint Top 5 decision over a bounded shortlist.

2. A retrieval-only execution mode that preserves abstract and PDF evidence assessment while omitting report-specific processing, exposed through local web, Python, CLI, and Notebook interfaces. 3. A three-system historical evaluation with explicit target-recovery, agreement, latency, token, and cost accounting, together with preserved prompts and outputs. 4. Optional implementation-analysis, citation-evolution, planning, benchmark-landscape, and citation-gap extensions, with their earlier exploratory evaluations distinguished from the retrieval benchmark.

Our comparison addresses finding papers from research ideas. It does not evaluate general website exploration, forum search, comprehensive web research, report quality, legal patent novelty, or the correctness of every citation recommendation. General web and forum capabilities remain limited. A designated-target miss can coexist with useful related papers, so target Hit@5 should be complemented by independently adjudicated relevance and usefulness.

Idea2Prior extends PaperArena with an auditable workflow for retrieving and ranking papers from research ideas. Joint ranking combines an abstract-level shortlist with bounded, explicitly partial PDF evidence, while a retrieval-only mode avoids report-specific work. In the documented historical comparison, aggregate reported Hit@5 is 53.3%, exceeding the two browser baselines overall, with a clear HARD-tier exception and longer reported latency. A separate historical cost sample averages $0.0945 per query. These findings motivate focused scholarly retrieval with inspectable evidence; they do not establish general Deep Research superiority, calibrated novelty assessment, or a matched baseline cost advantage.

inspect:2611.06598.question: In the LoRA fine-tuning experiments, how is behavioral compression rate measured, which adapter-compression baselines and held-out behavior tests are used, and how well do correction spectra predict rate across base models and noisy datasets?

passages.text: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) adapts a frozen language model through a compact learned update, making it a natural setting for asking how much information fine-tuning needs to write. Yet adapter rank, parameter count, or numerical reconstruction error do not directly tell us how many bits are required to preserve the acquired behavior. We therefore define an operational behavioral rate R ⋆ R^{\star} as the smallest serialized size of a compressed adapter that, once reloaded into the frozen base model, retains a fixed fraction of its held-out fine-tuning gain. Across LoRA fine-tuning experiments, this rate increases with distinct training content at fixed optimization budgets, but is not determined by intuitive metrics like source description length, fine-tuning gain, or weight-space reconstruction error. Most importantly, the same datasets exhibit substantially different, and even reordered, rates across frozen base models, showing that fine-tuning compressibility is a property of the dataset–receiver pair rather than of the dataset alone. However, we show that correction spectra measured on the data are able to rank these rates within a receiver. Finally, we study a striking noise-reducing effect of compression: adapters trained on deliberately corrupted datasets fall far below the frozen model, yet after compression score above it (23.7% to 82.9% on GSM8K, against 77.6% for frozen Qwen2.5-7B), consistently across tested families and sizes. The damage is unevenly concentrated in the adapter’s leading singular directions, which compression appears to filter. Away from its training task, the compressed corrupted adapter also generalizes better than a clean fine-tune: on harder math it retains 97% of base accuracy, versus 44% for the clean adapter. Together, these results

raining task, the compressed corrupted adapter also generalizes better than a clean fine-tune: on harder math it retains 97% of base accuracy, versus 44% for the clean adapter. Together, these results suggest that the information cost of fine-tuning depends on the receiver, target behavior, and how the required corrections are represented in the learned update.

evidence.quote: Across models with 124 124 M to 500 500 M parameters, it lowers effective rank [ Roy and Vetterli, 2007 ] and improves compression and inference speed at matched validation loss.

selections.summary: ORCA applies temporary soft orthogonality regularization early in LLM training, then removes it. The reported final validation-loss advantage over Muon extends across LLaMA, Qwen3, and MoE settings.

Across three agent models and three benchmarks, CORE achieves higher answer accuracy and evidence recall than Tongyi DeepResearch and OpenResearcher in every model–benchmark comparison, while returning substantially fewer tokens per search than Tongyi DeepResearch.

candidates.abstract_excerpt: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) has become the standard method for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large pretrained models, yet theoretical explanations for why low-rank updates suffice remain incomplete. Most existing analyses rely on the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) regime, which linearizes the network around the pretrained weights. In this work, we take a different approach that requires no linearization: our key observation is that, once the backbone is frozen, the loss sees each adapted weight matrix only through a finite-rank linear map induced by the frozen activations. Trace-norm regularization then forces the optimizer to pick a low-rank matrix among all matrices that produce the same observed output. candidates.title: A Riemannian Geometry for Low-rank Adaptation
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) is widely used as a parameter-efficient fine-tuning technique for pre-trained deep neural networks, which approximates the weight update via full fine-tuning by a low-rank matrix $BA^\top$. This parameterization leads to the equivalence relation $(B, A) \sim (BG^{-1}, AG^\top)$ for any invertible matrix $G$ because $BA^\top = BG^{-1}(AG^\top)^\top$ and thus both pairs yield the same loss value. This relation induces a quotient manifold where matrices $(BG^{-1}, AG^\top)$ for all $G$ are identified, eliminating redundant directions along which the loss value remains unchanged. To respect the geometry of this manifold, the original search space is endowed with a Riemannian metric that is invariant under the equivalence relation. Such a metric induces preconditioning at each gradient step and ensures that each weight update via LoRA changes the loss value, leading to efficient optimization. In this paper, we propose a new Riemannian metric that is specifically tailored to LoRA to close the gap to full fine-tuning at the weight level. candidates.title: Maximizing Capacity Utilization of LoRA Adapters for Mitigating the Learning-Forgetting Trade-off
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) often underperforms full fine-tuning, especially in heterogeneous and continual-learning settings in which substantial forgetting occurs. In general, it suffers from an undesirable learning-forgetting trade-off across diverse fine-tuning settings. We identify a potential contributor: LoRA adapters, especially high-rank ones, frequently fail to realize the available capacity afforded by the configured rank. Specifically, we find that standard LoRA updates have effective rank far below their configured rank, limiting how broadly the update energy is distributed. Therefore, we propose training mechanisms that optimize the original objective while maximizing adapter effective rank. Our main method adds a simple, stable, differentiable, and SVD-free Rényi-2 effective-rank regularizer to the language-modeling loss. We also connect capacity maximization to norm-bounded updates. candidates.abstract_excerpt: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is often highly sensitive to learning-rate (LR) choices. Recent empirical studies suggest that, once LRs are carefully tuned, vanilla LoRA can remain competitive with many proposed LoRA variants. This shifts the central practical question from designing ever more variants to reducing the cost and brittleness of LR selection. LoRA+ addresses this issue with asymmetric LRs, using a larger LR for the up-projection matrix $B$ than for the down-projection matrix $A$. However, the ratio $η_B / η_A$ itself becomes an additional hyperparameter: large ratios can improve adaptation, but under the standard LoRA initialization they can also cause unstable training and ratio-dependent performance collapse. We identify the source of this brittleness through a signal--noise decomposition of LoRA dynamics. candidates.title: Normalize-Then-Precondition: A Hierarchical Approach to Marginal Scale and Interaction Geometry for LLM Training
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Matrix optimizers have emerged as a promising direction, with Muon standing out as a prominent design. Revisiting Muon through its full-Gram representation, we observe that it jointly processes marginal-scale and interaction information. This opens an alternative way to organize geometric information hierarchically, motivating the Normalize-Then-Precondition framework. candidates.title: Rotated Manifold Optimization for Low-Rank Adaptation
candidates.abstract_excerpt: We propose a novel optimizer for low-rank adaptation (LoRA) that explicitly incorporates the gauge symmetry of low-rank factorization. Our optimizer extends recent matrix optimizers for full-parameter training to the manifold of fixed-rank matrices by interpreting them as normalization under a rotated basis. We show how rotation and normalization can be integrated with the fixed-rank manifold efficiently. Our optimizer converges faster to lower held-out loss and achieves better or comparable downstream performance on both supervised finetuning and reinforcement learning tasks.

candidates.title: Beyond Low-Rank Parameterization: Narrowing the Gap Between LoRA and Full Fine-Tuning via Gradient Decomposition
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is a widely used approach to parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT), yet a performance gap can remain relative to full fine-tuning (FFT). Many LoRA variants improve the initialization or optimization of low-rank factors. At each training step, however, their first-order weight-space directions are constrained by the current parameterization. We characterize the corresponding LoRA-accessible gradient space and show that it coincides with the tangent space induced by the current LoRA parameterization. candidates.title: Robust Parameter-Efficient LLM Adaptation on Analog Hardware

candidates.title: LoGRA: Scaling LLM Reinforcement Learning with Low-Rank Gradient Sketches
candidates.abstract_excerpt: Reinforcement learning has greatly advanced the capabilities of large language models, but its memory demands remain a barrier to broader adoption. candidates.title: Ori: Drift-Aware Streaming $k$-PCA for Very Low-Rank LLM Training
candidates.abstract_excerpt: A prominent family of low-rank LLM optimizers, pioneered by GaLore, performs gradient-subspace projection: at each step, they project the gradient into a low-dimensional subspace and map the update back to the full model. 2610.22794:b8146b2c89a9ea39b753053b63e65.question: In the 1B LLaMA pretraining experiments, what are Ori's measured peak GPU memory, throughput or step time, and validation-loss results versus GaLore and full-rank optimizers at matched rank and training budget?

passages.text: A prominent family of low-rank LLM optimizers, pioneered by GaLore, performs gradient-subspace projection: at each step, they project the gradient into a low-dimensional subspace and map the update back to the full model. Most existing work either recomputes the gradient subspace at certain intervals, or performs post-hoc adaptation to catch up to the moving subspace. In this work, we explicitly identify in practice the slow, stable manner in which LLM gradient subspaces drift across time. To this end, we propose Ori, a novel low-rank optimizer for training LLMs that captures the shifting principal gradient directions over time to achieve state-of-the-art accuracy under stringent low-rank constraints. Ori employs a streaming k k -PCA algorithm inspired by Oja++, whose low per-step cost enables high-frequency, on-the-fly subspace tracking. In practice, Ori reduces the performance gap of the state-of-the-art low-rank optimizers to full-rank optimizers by up to 69.3% on a 1B LLaMA pretraining task, and achieves the best performance on 10 out of 16 task scenarios in Roberta-Base fine-tuning. Together, these contributions allow Ori to further push the performance and efficiency frontiers of gradient-projecting optimizers, narrowing the gap to full-rank training for LLMs. Code can be found at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/Ori-Submission-2132 . 2 2 footnotetext: Purdue Institute for Cancer Research, Purdue University. 3 3 footnotetext: Department of Comparative Pathobiology, Purdue University.

We evaluate Ori’s pre-training performance against the baselines on the C4 dataset [ 26 ] using LLaMA-architecture models of four sizes (60M, 130M, 350M, and 1B), following similar experimental settings as prior work [ 14 , 39 ] . Departing from prior work that often tests a single rank, we systematically evaluate all low-rank methods across three distinct ranks for each model (e.g., r ∈ { 512,128 , 32 } r\in\{512,128,32\} for the 1B model), enabling a rigorous assessment of optimizer performance under varying degrees of memory constraints. To ensure a fair comparison, model hyperparameters were held constant for each model size, while each optimizer’s learning rate was tuned from { 0.01 , 0.005 , 0.001 , 0.0005 , 0.0001 } \{0.01,0.005,0.001,0.0005,0.0001\} . We report validation perplexity after a fixed token budget, with full details provided in Appendix E .

As shown in Table 1 , Ori’s performance is consistently strong, particularly in memory-constrained scenarios. At higher, less restrictive ranks (e.g., r = 128 r=128 for the 60M model, r = 256 r=256 for the 130M model), Ori performs on par with GaLore, establishing it as a highly competitive method in common low-rank settings. However, Ori’s distinct advantage emerges when the rank r r is severely constrained, where it demonstrates the most robust performance as its accuracy degrades the least under memory pressure. This trend, where the cost of a stale subspace projection becomes most apparent, is consistent across all model scales. For instance, when training the 130M model at an aggressively low rank of just 16, Ori achieves a validation perplexity of 43.61, substantially outperforming GaLore (60.29) and OSD (54.05). This result empirically validates our central hypothesis: actively tracking the gradient subspace drift is most critical when the optimizer has the fewest dimensions to work with. By excelling in these challenging low-rank regimes, Ori consistently narrows the performance gap to full-rank Adam, pushing the performance boundaries of memory-efficient optimization.

passages.section: E.8 Measuring optimizer state peak memory
passages.text: Finally, we report our procedure for measuring the memory footprint of the optimizers evaluated in our experiments. Our goal is to record the peak memory usage, incurred solely by the said optimizer’s update step. To this end, we take advantage of PyTorch’s memory recording functionalities. The below code listing shows the pseudocode for recording peack memory usage incurred solely by the optimizer’s step() operations. We use this procedure to obtain all the results in Tables 9 and 11 . Python code for profiling optimizer peak memory. ⬇ import torch # Model and optimizer setup model = … optimizer = … # Main training loop for batch in enumerate ( dataloader ): # Forward and backward pass loss = model (** batch ). loss loss . backward () # Record the current memory usage after model backward mem_after_backward = torch . cuda . memory_allocated () # Reset the max memory counter torch . cuda . reset_peak_memory_stats () # Optimizer step optimizer . step () # Read the optimizer-incurred max memory # The difference with mem_after_backward is the # maximum additional memory caused by optimizer.step() peak_mem_during_step = torch . cuda . max_memory_allocated () optim_peak_mem = peak_mem_during_step - mem_after_backward

Table 9 : Memory and Wallclock Time Comparison between Ori and non-error-feedback baselines (Adam, ReLoRA, GaLore, OSD). Analysis is conducted by pre-training 1B LLaMA on C4 dataset. Optimizer rank r = 512 r=512 r = 128 r=128 r = 32 r=32 Optimizer State Peak Memory (GB) Adam 2.4942 2.4942 2.4942 ReLoRA [ 14 ] 1.1349 0.4670 0.3000 GaLore [ 39 ] 0.3385 0.3385 0.3385 OSD [ 15 ] 0.2832 0.2832 0.2832 Ori (Ours) 0.2583 0.2506 0.2487 Average Update Time (s / Step) Adam 12.6015 12.6015 12.6015 ReLoRA [ 14 ] 13.9454 11.9193 11.5661 GaLore [ 39 ] 12.9699 12.9703 13.0401 OSD [ 15 ] 12.8438 12.8373 12.8594 Ori (Ours) 12.7266 12.7206 12.6705 Table 10 : Memory and Wallclock Time Comparison between O-LDAdam and an error-feedback baseline, LDAdam. Analysis is conducted by pre-training 1B LLaMA on C4 dataset. Optimizer rank r = 512 r=512 r = 128 r=128 r = 32 r=32 Optimizer State Peak Memory (GB) LDAdam ( T = 1 T=1 ) 0.1221 0.1221 0.1221 LDAdam ( T = 200 T=200 ) 0.1221 0.1221 0.1221 O-LDAdam (Ours) 0.1221 0.1221 0.1221 Average Update Time (s / Step) LDAdam ( T = 1 T=1 ) 13.9294 13.3475 13.1410 LDAdam ( T = 200 T=200 ) 12.7141 12.6996 12.6863 O-LDAdam (Ours) 13.4735 12.9018 12.8648

We profile the optimizer state peak memory and wall-clock time during the pre-training experiments from Section 5.2 . Details on the memory profiling procedure can be found in Section E.8 . As shown in Table 9 , Ori exhibits a superior efficiency profile among standard, non-error-feedback gradient-subspace methods (Adam, ReLoRA, GaLore, OSD). In addition, as shown in Table 10 , O-LDAdam demonstrates competitive and comparable efficiency profile to the error-feedback baseline LDAdam under the large update frequency regime ( T = 200 T=200 ). Full table on pre-training of other model sizes can be found in Appendix F . Memory Usage: Compared to standard, non-error-feedback baselines, Ori consistently consumes the least optimizer peak memory across all ranks. For instance, at rank 32, Ori requires only 0.2487 GB, which is 12.1% less than OSD (0.2832 GB) and 26.5% less than GaLore (0.3385 GB). This confirms Ori’s tangible memory savings. On the other hand, compared to the error-feedback methods, O-LDAdam consistently yields the same memory footprint as LDAdam baselines. Training Speed: Despite updating its subspace projector 10x more frequently ( T Ori = 20 T_{\text{Ori}}=20 vs. T GaLore/OSD = 200 T_{\text{GaLore/OSD}}=200 ), Ori is still the fastest among all standard, non-error-feedback methods. While the weight-subspace method ReLoRA is faster at lower ranks due to its different update mechanism, its worse model performance (see Table 1 ) highlights a clear trade-off. In contrast, Ori achieves superior model performance without compromising on speed, making it a more effective and efficient choice overall. The lightweight nature of the Oja++ update allows Ori to be both more accurate and faster than its direct competitors, making it a better choice for efficient training.

2610.11730:038c227b5397e1a001d6372646dae.question: For the LLaMA 124M–500M experiments, how were spectral weight decay and standard weight decay matched for validation loss and training compute, and what SVD-LLM compression baselines and distortion measurements support the reported gains?

passages.text: BRAIn Lab Spectral Weight Decay: Inducing Low-Rank Structure in Neural Network Weights Dmitrii Andriianov 1 , Andrey Veprikov 1,2 , Aleksandr Beznosikov 1,3 1 Basic Research of Artificial Intelligence Laboratory (BRAIn Lab) 2 SB AI Lab 3 Innopolis University Standard weight decay treats each weight matrix as a vector and ignores its spectral structure. We introduce spectral weight decay, a post-step decoupled nuclear-norm update that applies additive rather than multiplicative spectral shrinkage. We connect the update to approximate proximal descent and show that its sensitivity to update order can exceed that of conventional ℓ 2 \ell_{2} weight decay near rank deficiency. Across LLaMA models with 124 124 M to 500 500 M parameters, spectral weight decay lowers effective rank and improves SVD-LLM compression at matched validation loss. At 500 500 M and a 4 % 4\% distortion budget, it reaches 1.89 × 1.89\times compression and 1.18 × 1.18\times GPU inference speedup, compared with 1.14 × 1.14\times and 1.01 × 1.01\times after standard weight decay. Under fixed-horizon training with 60 % 60\% label noise, it also improves final mean clean-test accuracy over matched ℓ 2 \ell_{2} regularization by up to 17.8 17.8 points on MNIST and 4.6 4.6 points across four BERT-base tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/brain-lab-research/SpectralWD .

To make the regularizer matrix-aware, we begin with the proximal interpretation of decoupled weight decay. To first order, its update is a proximal gradient step for the squared Frobenius penalty [ Parikh and Boyd, 2014 ; Zhuang et al., 2022 ] . We replace this penalty with the nuclear norm, a convex surrogate for rank whose proximal operator soft-thresholds singular values [ Recht et al., 2010 ; Cai et al., 2010 ] . This construction is the matrix analogue of replacing ridge shrinkage with coefficient selection by the lasso [ Hoerl and Kennard, 1970 ; Tibshirani, 1996 ] . Given the loss-only optimizer direction Δ \Delta , let Z = W ( k ) − η ​ Δ = U Z ​ Σ Z ​ V Z ⊤ Z=W^{(k)}-\eta\Delta=U_{Z}\Sigma_{Z}V_{Z}^{\top} . Spectral weight decay applies the post-step correction W ( k + 1 ) = Z − η ​ λ ​ U Z ​ V Z ⊤ , W^{(k+1)}=Z-\eta\lambda U_{Z}V_{Z}^{\top}, (1) where η \eta is the learning rate and λ \lambda the regularization coefficient. This correction acts additively in the singular basis of Z Z , whereas conventional weight decay scales the spectrum uniformly. SLORR-Nuc also approximates the nuclear-norm polar factor [ González-Martínez and Liu, 2026 ] . Its decoupled extension would use the pre-step correction Z − η ​ λ ​ U W ​ V W ⊤ Z-\eta\lambda U_{W}V_{W}^{\top} for W ( k ) = U W ​ Σ W ​ V W ⊤ W^{(k)}=U_{W}\Sigma_{W}V_{W}^{\top} , rather than ( 1 ).

The additive shrinkage acts more strongly on smaller singular values and concentrates the spectrum. The resulting low-effective-rank weights admit efficient truncated SVD compression. Replacing a dense m × n m\times n matrix with rank- r r factors reduces its parameter count and multiplication cost from m ​ n mn to r ⁡ ( m + n ) r(m+n) . This factorization lowers storage and inference memory and can reduce latency when the retained rank is sufficiently small. Beyond compression, we test whether the same low-rank bias limits memorization under label noise. We evaluate spectral weight decay in LLaMA [ Touvron et al., 2023 ] pretraining, post-training compression, and fixed-horizon noisy-label classification. Across models with 124 124 M to 500 500 M parameters, it lowers effective rank [ Roy and Vetterli, 2007 ] and improves compression and inference speed at matched validation loss. At 500 500 M and a 4 % 4\% distortion budget, it reaches 1.89 × 1.89\times compression and a 1.18 × 1.18\times GPU inference speedup. At 60 % 60\% label noise, mean clean-test accuracy gains over matched ℓ 2 \ell_{2} regularization reach 17.78 17.78 points on MNIST and 4.59 4.59 points on four BERT-base tasks.

SliceGPT removes rows and columns after a principal-component transformation [ Ashkboos et al., 2024 ] . ASVD [ Yuan et al., 2023 ] and SVD-LLM [ Wang et al., 2024 ] use activation statistics to improve the factorization. Dobi-SVD learns layerwise truncation and reconstructs weights from truncated activations [ Wang et al., 2025 ] . Prehab fine-tunes a trained model for SVD compression [ Qin et al., 2025 ] . Appendix B.2 compares spectral weight decay with Prehab in this setting. Our main experiments apply it throughout pretraining and evaluate compression and inference with SVD-LLM. Appendix B.4 compares post-training compression methods. Section 3 shows the resulting compression and inference gains.

Spectral weight decay lowers the effective rank of weight matrices, making them amenable to low-rank compression. We use SVD-LLM [ Wang et al., 2024 ] , which gives the lowest validation loss in our matched comparison. We compress each weight matrix to its own effective rank, which varies substantially across layers (Figure 2 , middle). We leave the token embeddings and output head uncompressed because their ranks respond little to spectral weight decay, and compressing them even to their effective ranks sharply degrades model quality. The comparison and compression procedure are described in Appendix B.4 . Figure 3 (top) reports the maximum compression rate supported by each validation-loss distortion budget. Spectral weight decay substantially shifts this frontier upward at all three model scales. For the 500 500 M model and a 4 % 4\% distortion budget, it supports 1.89 × 1.89\times compression, compared with 1.14 × 1.14\times after standard weight decay. The same factorization reduces the FLOPs of a linear layer when r ⁡ ( m + n ) < m ​ n r(m+n)<mn . This reduction does not translate directly into lower latency because the factorized forward pass evaluates ( U r ​ Σ r ) ​ ( V r ⊤ ​ X ) (U_{r}\Sigma_{r})(V_{r}^{\top}X) with two GEMMs instead of the single GEMM W ​ X WX . The additional kernel launch and intermediate activation can offset the reduction in FLOPs. To improve tensor-core utilization, we round the effective rank down to the nearest multiple of 16 16 , r l = max ⁡ ( 16 , 16 ​ ⌊ erank ⁡ ( W l ) 16 ⌋ ) , r_{l}=\max\!\left(16,\,16\left\lfloor\frac{\operatorname{erank}(W_{l})}{16}\right\rfloor\right), (3)

Adjusting an aligned rank by one step, ± 16 \pm 16 , has negligible effect on validation loss. We therefore use this rank-aligned compression scheme throughout. The factorized models outperform their dense counterparts only at large batch sizes, so we measure forward-pass latency with a batch size of 256 256 on a single GPU. For the 500 500 M model, spectral weight decay yields a 1.09 × 1.09\times speedup near a 2 % 2\% distortion budget and reaches 1.18 × 1.18\times at 4 % 4\% , compared with 1.01 × 1.01\times under standard weight decay (Figure 3 , bottom).

2610.06116:7cd7f8e4ed04b9841003c0b7e07b1.question: Across the LLaMA, Qwen3, and MoE pretraining experiments, what are ORCA's validation-loss gains versus Muon and Adam at matched training budgets, and what measured training-time or memory overhead does temporary orthogonality regularization add?

passages.text: Modern LLM optimizers such as Muon often produce weight matrices with higher effective rank than Adam, yet further spectral control has delivered only modest gains. We identify a tension behind this result: concentrated spectra can suppress gradient directions in coupled weight matrices and slow optimization, while constraints maintained throughout training can limit task-specific adaptation and raise the attainable loss floor. We introduce ORCA (Orthogonal Regularization, Cooled After), a minimal optimizer intervention that applies strong but temporary soft orthogonality regularization early in training, then removes it. This allows the weights to benefit from a broader spectrum early on and adapt freely afterward. Across LLaMA, Qwen3, and fine-grained mixture-of-experts models ranging from 130M to 8B parameters, ORCA achieves lower final validation loss than Muon. Its loss reduction relative to Muon matches or exceeds Muon’s reduction relative to Adam. Ablations support the early-shaping, later-release design. Further, ORCA requires no architectural changes and adds minimal overhead. An implementation is available at https://github.com/uuurraaa/ORCA_Optimizer .

However, we argue that this trade-off is not fundamental. Spectral regularization may be most valuable early, when it can shape the optimization trajectory, yet become a liability if maintained as the weights adapt to the task. The two effects need not be accepted together: we can use the constraint to shape the spectrum, then release it before it restricts the final solution. This motivates a minimal method ORCA (Orthogonal Regularization, Cooled After): During an initial phase, ORCA applies a soft orthogonality penalty, R orth ​ ( 𝐖 ) = 1 4 ​ ‖ 𝐖𝐖 ⊤ − 𝐈 ‖ F 2 R_{\mathrm{orth}}(\mathbf{W})=\frac{1}{4}\|\mathbf{W}\mathbf{W}^{\top}-\mathbf{I}\|_{F}^{2} . Then directly removes it at a single switch point. Training thereafter follows the standard optimizer update, with no gradual decay or further changes. This design lets early regularization influence the optimization path without prescribing the spectrum throughout training. In our experiments, this simple release is followed by faster loss reduction and a lower final validation loss than Muon. Figure 1.1: LLaMA 130M training dynamics. Effective rank is measured on a middle-layer V V projection; the dashed line marks regularization release. Figure 1.1 illustrates the transition. While the penalty is active, the effective rank of the weight matrix rises sharply above Muon’s, although ORCA initially has a higher validation loss. After release, the rank falls from its peak but remains above Muon’s, while validation loss decreases rapidly, crosses the Muon curve. The result is consistent with early spectral shaping leaving a useful effect on the subsequent trajectory, even after the explicit penalty is gone. Controlled interventions in Section 5 further investigates into this connection.

We evaluate ORCA on LLaMA, Qwen3, and fine-grained MoE models ranging from 130M to 8B parameters, including 100B-token training runs. ORCA achieves lower final validation loss than Muon across these settings. In most experiments, the reduction is 0.02–0.04, comparable to or greater than Muon’s gain over Adam. To put this loss reduction in perspective, on LLaMA 1.3B, ORCA achieving the 0.024 lower validation loss reaches Muon’s 100k-step loss in just 60k steps. Further, downstream evaluations, alternative early spectral interventions, multi-seed runs, and ablations of method parameters and intervention timing further support these gains. Together, these results show that early spectral shaping followed by constraint relaxation can improve training efficiency and final performance across architectures without substantial changes to the optimizer. To summarize the contributions of the paper: (1) We illustrate a trade-off in spectral control through a simplified model and empirical observations: favorable spectra can accelerate optimization but persistent constraints may harm the attainable solution quality. (2) We introduce ORCA, a minimal shape-then-release optimizer that leverages early orthogonal regularization to improve optimization trajectories while allowing unconstrained adaptation in later training. (3) We demonstrate ORCA’s effectiveness across diverse LLM architectures and scales, achieving faster convergence and lower loss than existing optimizers. Through extensive controlled experiments, we further validate the mechanism that early effective-rank shaping drives the observed improvements.

We also evaluate how the optimization performance translates into token efficiency by measuring the training required to reach a common target loss. We continued ORCA from its original 51k-step checkpoint, starting the final decay early, and reached a validation loss of 2.318 at approximately 60k steps. The standard Muon run, using its original 100k-step settings, reached the same loss at 100k steps ( Figure 2(a) ). Therefore, ORCA used 40% fewer tokens to reach this target, a 1.66× token-efficiency gain. To save compute, we reused the checkpoint without retuning ORCA for the shorter run: its original 25k-step shaping stage accounts for 41.7% of the 60k-step budget rather than the tuned default of 25%. 2611.17191:9e4a010c9ee4b0add839a37291853.question: In language-model LoRA rank sweeps, what effective-rank, validation-perplexity, and forgetting results does the Rényi-2 regularizer achieve versus unpenalized LoRA at matched rank and training budget? What seeds and baselines support the comparison?

passages.text: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) often underperforms full fine-tuning, especially in heterogeneous and continual-learning settings in which substantial forgetting occurs. In general, it suffers from an undesirable learning–forgetting trade-off across diverse fine-tuning settings. We identify a potential contributor: LoRA adapters, especially high-rank ones, frequently fail to realize the available capacity afforded by the configured rank. Specifically, we find that standard LoRA updates have effective rank far below their configured rank, limiting how broadly the update energy is distributed. Therefore, we propose training mechanisms that optimize the original objective while maximizing adapter effective rank. Our main method adds a simple, stable, differentiable, and SVD-free Rényi-2 effective-rank regularizer to the language-modeling loss. We also connect capacity maximization to norm-bounded updates. In mixed-domain rank sweeps on three models evaluated with multiple random seeds, a penalty weight of λ = 0.01 \lambda=0.01 lowers mean Wiki perplexity at every tested rank of at least 16 16 relative to unpenalized LoRA. Mean training perplexity improves or increases by at most 0.02 0.02 in all but one model–rank comparison. Single-task and scheduling experiments further show that the balance between learning and retention depends on the configuration. We also observe that several LoRA variants in the literature also suffer from the identified capacity issue, and our approach provides a complementary axis of improvement to LoRA-based parameter-efficient fine-tuning. These results suggest that effective rank is not only a post-hoc diagnostic of adapter quality, but a trainable objective for improving the learning–forgetting frontier. Our code is available at

passages.text: Across the reported mixed-domain rank sweeps on Qwen2.5-0.5B, Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct, and Llama-3.2-3B-Instruct, λ = 0.01 \lambda=0.01 lowers mean Wiki perplexity relative to unpenalized LoRA at every tested rank of at least 16 16 (Tables 9 , 10 , and 11 ). Mean Train PPL improves or increases by at most 0.020 0.020 in all but one of these comparisons; the exception is Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct at r = 16 r=16 , where it increases from 4.211 4.211 to 4.524 4.524 . These results support a consistent Wiki retention benefit in this setting, but not universal improvement on both objectives.

Standard LoRA training often underutilizes its allocated subspace so nominal rank is an unreliable proxy for usable adapter capacity in the learning–forgetting trade-off. We proposed effective-rank maximization via the Rényi-2 penalty, a parameterization-agnostic, SVD-free term added to the language-modeling loss, and showed across mixed-domain SFT, task-specific SFT, rank sweeps, and scheduling ablations that it can reduce forgetting on pretraining proxies while maintaining competitive target-task fit. In mixed-domain rank sweeps on three models, λ = 0.01 \lambda=0.01 lowers mean Wiki perplexity at every tested rank of at least 16 16 relative to unpenalized LoRA, with mean Train PPL improving or increasing by at most 0.02 0.02 in all but one comparison. Our single-task and scheduling experiments also demonstrate configuration-dependent learning and retention outcomes: the penalty can improve retention without a large training-fit cost, but does not eliminate the learning–forgetting trade-off. Spectral diagnostics provide descriptive comparisons of the resulting updates. Effective rank is therefore not merely a post-hoc diagnostic but a trainable objective that regularizes toward fuller utilization.

Unless a table caption states otherwise, all numbers are taken from the terminal training state of a completed run; we do not reload an in-run best-validation checkpoint. Early stopping is disabled. Periodic evals run every 100 100 optimizer steps; perplexity and forgetting probes below are the values logged at the last eval before the run hits its token or epoch budget. Train PPL is exp ⁡ ( H ) \exp(H) where H H is an exponential moving average ( β = 0.99 \beta{=}0.99 ) of the assistant-only training loss; it is a smoothed training-loss proxy, not held-out validation perplexity. Wiki PPL and StarCoder PPL are reference-probe perplexities on fixed OLMo-Mix-1124 slices, using the plain-text supervision protocol and batch limits specified above. In the mixed-domain setting we additionally log in-mixture retention probes on held-out GSM8K and WMT19 Czech–English validation text; Appendix Table 5 reports both in-mixture probes. eRank is the Roy–Vetterli effective rank of the accumulated adapter update Δ ​ W \Delta W , averaged over all targeted down_proj modules, taken from the last logged rank diagnostic. This is distinct from the Rényi-2 surrogate used in the objective. Dense down-projection fine-tuning baselines select hyperparameters via a separate sweep (Section F.1 ), but reported metrics still refer to the terminal state of the selected run. Post-hoc spectral analyses (intruder dimensions, subspace alignment, singular-direction mixing) use measurements from the final saved checkpoint.

2610.04507:b593ca751c856d37070bc34a0bac1.question: In the noisy-label rank sweeps, how are LoRA and dense fine-tuning matched by trainable modules, seed, optimizer, and training budget? What are the 7B language-model results for clean-test generalization and noisy-label memorization across ranks, and how do they compare with the vision results?

passages.text: Double descent has sparked considerable interest, with recent work relating it to the data, the model and the learning configuration. Practical fine-tuning commonly involves training a small adapter on top of frozen pretrained weights, as in low-rank adaptation (LoRA). The adapter’s rank is the hyperparameter that sets its capacity, yet how this rank relates to double descent has not been well explored. We quantify this relation under label noise on four vision backbones and a 7 7 B language model with a module-matched rank sweep (MMRS), which extends past full rank and compares every rank with dense fine-tuning of the same modules, paired by seed. On DeiT-Tiny, risk is lowest at rank one and rises sharply as the adapter becomes able to fit the noisy labels, forming an interpolation cliff. Past the peak, risk falls again, but every tested post-peak rank that still saves parameters remains above dense risk. Rank-one LoRA outperforms dense fine-tuning on three of the four vision backbones, consistent with strong regularization at small rank. LoRA thus exhibits a second descent, but matches dense risk only after losing its parameter advantage, first on DeiT-Tiny at four times dense’s projection weights. Code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/lora-second-descent-C7B5 .

Unless noted, this section uses an ImageNet-pretrained DeiT-Tiny on 5 5 k-example CIFAR-100 subsets with 20 % 20\% symmetric label noise and LoRA on the fused query-key-value (qkv) projections of the last six blocks (full protocol in Section 5.1 ). Risk rises where the adapter begins to fit noise. Test NLL is minimized at r = 1 r{=}1 , below that of the linear probe, so a single rank of adaptation already beats frozen features. The curve then climbs steeply and peaks at r = 64 r{=}64 , 0.53 0.53 nats above the minimum (Figure 2 a). Train accuracy locates the climb: it crosses 99 % 99\% between r = 16 r{=}16 and r = 24 r{=}24 , so risk rises exactly as ranks acquire the ability to fit the noisy training set within budget (Figure 5 ). With clean labels the shape flattens into a mild monotone rise; label noise amplifies this peak as it does the classical one ( Nakkiran et al., 2020 ) . Where classical double descent would begin descending, the noisy curve instead keeps rising to r = 64 r{=}64 , and accuracy tells the same story, still below its rank-one level at r = 4 ​ d r{=}4d (Table 8 ). The pipeline does produce textbook double descent. From-scratch ResNet-18 width sweeps, run with the same data loading, noise injection, optimizer family and evaluation, peak in the interior and then carry risk below their own pre-peak valley, by 0.196 0.196 nats on CIFAR-10 and, on the identical CIFAR-100 subsets used for fine-tuning, by 0.658 0.658 nats, in every seed on both datasets (Figure 7 ). Dataset, sample size and noise draw are not what slows the second descent.

The rank axis does run a second descent, and a sweep that stops at full rank can miss it. Judging what this descent is worth requires a reference point, which the module-matched rank sweep supplies by grading every setting against dense fine-tuning of the identical modules with the trainable-parameter ratio beside it. Across four vision backbones and a 7 7 B language model, no measured post-peak rank that still saves parameters reaches dense, and the first equivalence result sits at four times dense’s projection weights under a single shared learning rate. Full rank supplies the expressivity, so the remaining gap is a matter of coordinates, which the frozen-factor interventions show can move risk by about the size of the gap. 2610.04249:a530c41eba3e4f2463de455e3d72b.question: What balance and alignment assumptions underlie the singular-mode results for GD, Muon, Shampoo, and Adam-like updates? Does the paper test whether those spectral predictions or low-rank bias hold in neural-network or language-model training beyond matrix factorization?

passages.text: Recent successes of matrix- and curvature-based optimizers have renewed interest in how update geometry shapes learning. These methods normalize or precondition updates, changing how different components progress during training. In deep matrix factorization, the geometry that slows gradient descent (GD) favors low-rank solutions by delaying the emergence of small singular modes. This raises the question of what remains of that spectral bias when normalization or curvature correction weakens or removes the slowdown. We study how optimizer geometry and depth jointly govern this behavior through a common framework for singular mode dynamics. Under explicit balance and alignment assumptions, we derive birth, saturation, and decay laws for Euclidean GD, coordinate-wise updates of SignGD and an instantaneous Adam approximation, spectral updates of Muon and cumulative Shampoo, and a block curvature model of K-FAC. The resulting picture is not a simple ordering from stronger to weaker low-rank bias. To highlight, SignGD and ideal Muon eliminate the divergent birth barrier and drive unsupported modes to zero in finite time. Cumulative Shampoo initially retains GD’s depth-dependent barrier, then accumulated gradients produce a catch-up phase while making previously active modes increasingly persistent. Undamped K-FAC cancels the factorization-induced slowdown while preserving the ordering of the target singular values, whereas positive damping introduces a spectral threshold below which the slow GD phase laws reappear. These results give normalization, accumulated state, damping, and depth a direct interpretation as controls determining when modes emerge, persist, and disappear during training.

Analyses of gradient flow and gradient descent connect spectral dynamics to low rank recovery and incremental rank growth under specified initialization and measurement assumptions ( Gunasekar et al., 2017 ; Arora et al., 2019 ; Li et al., 2021 ; Jin et al., 2023 ) . While depth strengthens the tendency of low rank bias, it is not always equivalent to minimizing a single Schatten norm, indicating that trajectory-level geometry is essential ( Razin and Cohen, 2020 ) . Recent Muon analyses characterize how polar normalization changes spectral learning and simplicity bias in deep linear networks and linear attention ( Dragutinović and Ranganath, 2026 ) , and establish approximately uniform singular value growth under assumptions on LoRA factorization ( Kang et al., 2026 ) . For fully observed bilinear matrix factorization, Rhee et al. (2026) derive uniform factor singular value growth after alignment, and analyze oscillations caused by finite optimization steps. Complementary empirical comparisons show that Muon’s relative performance depends on the factorization problem and hyperparameter tuning ( Parviz et al., 2026 ) . Shampoo has been interpreted as an adapted version of spectral descent that retains information about stochasticity and the parameter trajectory ( Eschenhagen et al., 2026 ) . Building on these results, we compare mode birth, decay, and saturation within a common balanced aligned model. While most analyses study one optimizer in isolation, our analysis includes SignGD and simplified Adam, derives an exact accumulator identity for cumulative Shampoo, and quantifies the effect of additive damping in K-FAC. We give a broader discussion on related works in App. A .

Our analysis shows that the spectral bias of depth depends on optimizer geometry and the stage of training. A surprising consequence is that rapid learning of weak components can coexist with rapid removal of unsupported ones, as illustrated by the Muon analysis. Conversely, accumulated history can accelerate the emergence of a mode while prolonging its persistence. These effects make a single ordering of optimizers by stronger or weaker low-rank bias inadequate. A further implication is that parameters associated with numerical stability also shape learning bias. In the analyzed models, Adam’s stabilizer, Shampoo’s accumulator initialization, and K-FAC’s damping determine where normalization, history, or curvature correction governs spectral progress. They can therefore change how strongly depth suppresses small modes, even within the same optimizer. Although the phase laws rely on balance and alignment assumptions, they identify concrete mechanisms to understand optimizer behavior. This perspective motivates evaluating optimizers through which components they accelerate, suppress, or preserve alongside the training loss, since comparable fit can conceal differences in their dynamics. The resulting framework provides a basis for understanding and testing how faster optimizers change the complexity of intermediate models.

passages.section: Analysis of Muon in matrix factorization.
passages.text: Kang et al. (2026) analyze spectral gradient flow in a simplified LoRA factorization setting, proving approximately equal spectral growth rates and convergence results under stated conditions. Dragutinović and Ranganath (2026) derive dynamics for simplified Muon in deep linear networks and linear attention and investigate how avoiding slow sequential learning changes simplicity bias. Rhee et al. (2026) analyze bilinear factorization with full observation, including uniform factor growth after alignment, a conserved quantity distinct from GD’s, and finite step oscillations near solutions. They also study alignment in simplified settings. These results already establish much of the ideal polar growth baseline. Our treatment places it alongside memory dependent adaptive flows and damped curvature flows, with separate statements for birth, saturation, and zero target decay. Parviz et al. (2026) report controlled optimizer comparisons showing that Muon’s relative performance in factorization depends on the problem and hyperparameter tuning. This motivates separating exact polar flow predictions from practical implementation effects and comparing recovery at a common training fit.

Muon updates each factor by orthogonalizing matrix updates, that is Z ℓ = U ℓ ​ V ℓ ⊤ Z_{\ell}=U_{\ell}V_{\ell}^{\top} . In the diagonal aligned singular mode model, G = diag ⁡ ( g i ) G=\mathrm{diag}(g_{i}) . Therefore, z i = sign ⁡ ( g i ) z_{i}=\sign(g_{i}) . Thus, for each mode σ ˙ \displaystyle\dot{\sigma} = − L ​ σ q ​ sign ⁡ ( g ) \displaystyle=-L\sigma^{q}\sign(g) = − L ​ σ q ​ sign ⁡ ( ( σ − μ ) ​ σ q ) \displaystyle=-L\sigma^{q}\sign((\sigma-\mu)\sigma^{q}) = − L ​ σ q ​ sign ⁡ ( σ − μ ) \displaystyle=-L\sigma^{q}\sign(\sigma-\mu) reducing it to a scalar sign rule as in SignGD updates. Therefore, Proposition 6 holds for Muon as well. Note that this is a spectral update in matrix space even though the aligned model reduces it to a scalar sign rule as in SignGD updates, and this does not mean Muon has the same global bias as coordinate SignGD. Coordinate SignGD is coordinate-basis dependent. Muon is matrix-basis / spectral-geometry dependent. But in an aligned diagonal model, both reduce to sign dynamics on singular modes. Therefore, Muon weakens low rank bias in the diagonal mode. It controls spectral geometry, not rank directly. A spectral-norm ball constrains the largest singular value, but it does not penalize the number of nonzero singular values. So Muon should not be expected to behave like nuclear-norm minimization.

Figure 8: Effect of depth on decay laws and Shampoo saturation order. Left: empirical decay exponents α d \alpha_{d} for unsupported modes as depth varies. All optimizers closely follow the theoretical predictions in general. Right: Shampoo saturation coefficient β \beta as a function of the positive target mode μ \mu for L ∈ { 2 , 4 , 8 } L\in\{2,4,8\} . Shampoo is singled out here because its saturation phase is where mode order reversal can happen theoretically. At L = 2 L=2 , β \beta decreases with μ \mu , so smaller target modes saturate faster. At L = 8 L=8 , the ordering reverses and larger target modes saturate faster, while L = 4 L=4 lies near the transition. These results show that depth influences not only the size of the phase law exponents, but also the ordering of mode fitting under optimizer state dynamics. Figs. 9 and 11 show the evolution of training loss and ranks throughout training for depths L = 2 L=2 and 8 8 , respectively. In both cases, all optimizers converge to similar rank and loss solutions. But their trajectory shows the difference. Similarly, Figs. 10 and 12 show the singular mode trajectories for L = 2 L=2 and 8 8 , respectively. In both cases, we observe that GD exhibits strong sequential learning and at the same time other optimizers also begin to show stronger bias with depth. All optimizers train the same depth L = 2 L=2 deep linear factorization toward the same rank eight target and reach comparable final training loss. Cumulative Shampoo initially retains GD’s depth-dependent barrier, then accumulated gradients produce a catch-up phase while making previously active modes increasingly persistent. Undamped K-FAC cancels the factorization-induced slowdown while preserving the ordering of the target singular values, whereas positive damping introduces a spectral threshold below which the slow GD phase laws reappear. These results give normalization, accumulated state, damping, and depth a direct interpretation as controls determining when modes emerge, persist, and disappear during training.

Analyses of gradient flow and gradient descent connect spectral dynamics to low rank recovery and incremental rank growth under specified initialization and measurement assumptions ( Gunasekar et al., 2017 ; Arora et al., 2019 ; Li et al., 2021 ; Jin et al., 2023 ) . While depth strengthens the tendency of low rank bias, it is not always equivalent to minimizing a single Schatten norm, indicating that trajectory-level geometry is essential ( Razin and Cohen, 2020 ) . Recent Muon analyses characterize how polar normalization changes spectral learning and simplicity bias in deep linear networks and linear attention ( Dragutinović and Ranganath, 2026 ) , and establish approximately uniform singular value growth under assumptions on LoRA factorization ( Kang et al., 2026 ) . For fully observed bilinear matrix factorization, Rhee et al. (2026) derive uniform factor singular value growth after alignment, and analyze oscillations caused by finite optimization steps. Complementary empirical comparisons show that Muon’s relative performance depends on the factorization problem and hyperparameter tuning ( Parviz et al., 2026 ) . Shampoo has been interpreted as an adapted version of spectral descent that retains information about stochasticity and the parameter trajectory ( Eschenhagen et al., 2026 ) . Building on these results, we compare mode birth, decay, and saturation within a common balanced aligned model. While most analyses study one optimizer in isolation, our analysis includes SignGD and simplified Adam, derives an exact accumulator identity for cumulative Shampoo, and quantifies the effect of additive damping in K-FAC. We give a broader discussion on related works in App. A .

Our analysis shows that the spectral bias of depth depends on optimizer geometry and the stage of training. A surprising consequence is that rapid learning of weak components can coexist with rapid removal of unsupported ones, as illustrated by the Muon analysis. Conversely, accumulated history can accelerate the emergence of a mode while prolonging its persistence. These effects make a single ordering of optimizers by stronger or weaker low-rank bias inadequate. A further implication is that parameters associated with numerical stability also shape learning bias. In the analyzed models, Adam’s stabilizer, Shampoo’s accumulator initialization, and K-FAC’s damping determine where normalization, history, or curvature correction governs spectral progress. They can therefore change how strongly depth suppresses small modes, even within the same optimizer. Although the phase laws rely on balance and alignment assumptions, they identify concrete mechanisms to understand optimizer behavior. This perspective motivates evaluating optimizers through which components they accelerate, suppress, or preserve alongside the training loss, since comparable fit can conceal differences in their dynamics. The resulting framework provides a basis for understanding and testing how faster optimizers change the complexity of intermediate models.

Kang et al. (2026) analyze spectral gradient flow in a simplified LoRA factorization setting, proving approximately equal spectral growth rates and convergence results under stated conditions. Dragutinović and Ranganath (2026) derive dynamics for simplified Muon in deep linear networks and linear attention and investigate how avoiding slow sequential learning changes simplicity bias. Rhee et al. (2026) analyze bilinear factorization with full observation, including uniform factor growth after alignment, a conserved quantity distinct from GD’s, and finite step oscillations near solutions. They also study alignment in simplified settings. These results already establish much of the ideal polar growth baseline. Our treatment places it alongside memory dependent adaptive flows and damped curvature flows, with separate statements for birth, saturation, and zero target decay. Parviz et al. (2026) report controlled optimizer comparisons showing that Muon’s relative performance in factorization depends on the problem and hyperparameter tuning. This motivates separating exact polar flow predictions from practical implementation effects and comparing recovery at a common training fit.

passages.text: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) is a widely used approach to parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT), yet a performance gap can remain relative to full fine-tuning (FFT). Many LoRA variants improve the initialization or optimization of low-rank factors. At each training step, however, their first-order weight-space directions are constrained by the current parameterization. We characterize the corresponding LoRA-accessible gradient space and show that it coincides with the tangent space induced by the current LoRA parameterization. This characterization yields an orthogonal decomposition of the full weight gradient at the current model parameters. We term the component orthogonal to this space the normal gradient . Based on this decomposition, we propose GDLoRA (Gradient-Decomposed Low-Rank Adaptation) . GDLoRA reconstructs the full weight gradient from forward activations and backward signals, extracts its normal component, and directly updates the base weights with this component, while retaining standard AdamW optimization for the LoRA factors. GDLoRA incorporates complementary normal gradients without increasing standard LoRA’s optimizer-state memory budget under matched adapter and optimizer configurations. Experiments on natural language understanding, mathematical reasoning, commonsense reasoning, and image classification show that GDLoRA consistently improves over LoRA and narrows the performance gap to FFT. The code is available at https://anonymous.4open.science/r/GDLoRA .

Given the increasing scale of foundation models, parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods have been extensively studied to reduce the computational and memory costs of model adaptation ( Houlsby et al., 2019 ; Li and Liang, 2021 ; Lester et al., 2021 ; Hu et al., 2021 ) . Instead of updating all parameters during fine-tuning, PEFT methods optimize only a small subset of additional parameters while keeping the pretrained model largely frozen. Existing PEFT methods can be broadly categorized into several groups. One line of research explores adapter-based tuning ( Houlsby et al., 2019 ; Pfeiffer et al., 2020 ) , which introduces lightweight trainable modules into pretrained networks and updates only these additional parameters during adaptation. Another line focuses on prompt-based tuning ( Li and Liang, 2021 ; Lester et al., 2021 ) , which adapts pretrained models by optimizing learnable prompts or virtual tokens without modifying the model parameters. In a related direction, Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) ( Hu et al., 2021 ) introduces trainable low-rank matrices into pretrained layers while keeping the base weights frozen, reducing the number of optimized parameters and the associated optimizer-state memory. In this work, we focus on improving the optimization capability of LoRA-based adaptation.

We presented GDLoRA, which complements standard LoRA with gradient information beyond the first-order directions accessible through its current parameterization. By characterizing the LoRA-accessible gradient space as the induced tangent space, GDLoRA isolates the normal component of the full weight gradient and applies it directly to the base weights, while retaining standard AdamW optimization for the adapters. Under matched adapter and optimizer configurations, GDLoRA preserves LoRA’s optimizer-state memory budget. Experiments on natural language understanding, mathematical reasoning, commonsense reasoning, and image classification demonstrate consistent improvements over LoRA and a reduced performance gap to FFT. Ablation studies further support the effectiveness of normal-gradient updates in complementing low-rank adaptation.

We compare GDLoRA with full fine-tuning (FFT), standard LoRA ( Hu et al., 2021 ) , Fira ( Chen et al., 2024 ) , and five LoRA variants: PiSSA ( Meng et al., 2024 ) , DoRA ( Liu et al., 2024 ) , rsLoRA ( Kalajdzievski, 2023 ) , LoRA-GA ( Wang et al., 2024 ) , and LoRA-Pro ( Wang et al., 2025 ) . FFT updates all model parameters during fine-tuning. The LoRA variants seek to narrow the performance gap between LoRA and FFT through improved initialization, weight parameterization, scaling, or optimization. During fine-tuning, their updates remain governed by their respective adapter parameterizations. Fira instead combines low-rank gradient projection with scaled residual updates to enable full-rank weight adaptation. GDLoRA supplements standard LoRA with normal-gradient updates applied directly to the base weights, extending adaptation beyond the first-order weight-space directions accessible through the current LoRA parameterization. 2610.10965:388def2792f5d58b6e45d81a2986b.question: In the NanoGPT experiments, how do Spectrally Targeted Muon variants compare with Muon and SGD on validation loss, effective rank, and training time at matched compute? Which spectral subspaces drive any improvement?

passages.text: The Muon optimizer orthogonalizes each update matrix, setting all of its singular values to one, and has proven highly effective for training large language models. It remains unclear, however, whether this success comes from amplifying small singular directions that gradient descent neglects or from suppressing large, degenerate directions that disrupt training. We introduce Spectrally Targeted Muon, which orthogonalizes only the singular values above or below a threshold τ \tau , so that varying τ \tau interpolates between normalized SGD and Muon. It isolates the relevant singular subspaces with projections computed by Newton-Schulz iteration on a shifted Gram matrix, so no SVD is needed. We evaluate these variants on the CIFAR-10 and NanoGPT speedruns, tracking the effective rank of gradient, update, and weight matrices and a new metric, the alignment of updates with the tangent space of the weight matrix’s isospectral manifold. We find three things. First, the small singular values of the momentum are not noise. Orthogonalizing everything except the few largest singular values of each matrix nearly matches Muon while touching only a small fraction of the momentum, whereas orthogonalizing only the top falls well short even though it holds almost all of it. On language models every momentum singular value is far below one, so targeted orthogonalization can only amplify, and Muon wins by making directions that are too small to train on at their raw scale trainable. Second, shrinking the largest singular values is what keeps the parameter spectrum flat; this is cheap, and it is not what drives the loss. Third, AdamW differs from Muon mainly in how slowly it builds structure, which explains its slower start and why warmup helps AdamW but only hurts Muon.

Figure 4: Effective rank of the gradient (a) and update (b), averaged over all matrices, and of the value (c), attention-output (d) and MLP (e) parameters, averaged over layers (seed 0). Dashed lines are the warmup variants, the dotted line in (a) marks the start of the learning rate cooldown, and the legend in (b) applies to all panels. We use the effective rank of the gradient and update matrix to help explain our optimizer performances. Since the gradient depends only on the surrounding loss landscape and not the optimizer, it tells us which optimizers enter parts of the loss landscape where many directions are available. This happens quickly for Muon and the targeted variants, while AdamW takes a few hundred steps to get there. During learning rate cooldown, this effective rank grows for every optimizer, because the leading singular values of the gradient shrink while its bulk stays put. In the river-valley picture of Wen et al. (2024) , the component of the gradient along the sharp valley walls dies with the learning rate while the component along the flat floor remains. Gradient rank thus tells us where the iterate sits in the valley, bouncing between the walls or settled on the floor. Meanwhile, the effective rank of the update shows the difference between the different types of targeting, with bottom targeting creating an update shaped like Muon’s, while top targeting creates an even lower rank update than AdamW. (a) Tangent alignment (b) Spectrum-changing update by singular direction (c) Final loss vs. parameter rank

Figure 5: How much of the update changes the spectrum, and where. (a) Log-barrier of the isospectral tangent fraction, averaged over matrices; the grey dotted line is the value for a random rotation, the orange dotted line marks the start of the learning rate cooldown, and dashed lines are the warmup variants. (b) Share of the spectrum-changing part of the update at each singular direction of the parameter, ranked by singular value, averaged over matrices and steps 100–1500; the dotted line is uniform. (c) Final validation loss against final parameter effective rank, including the learning rate controls; the bottom-targeted runs at τ ≤ 4 × 10 − 4 \tau\leq 4\times 10^{-4} leave their MLP output matrices barely trained. Next, we examined the parameter effective ranks across different types of Transformer parameters in Figure 4 (c)–(e). We were able to observe the same results as Wang et al. (2025) , who found that AdamW heavily reduces the effective rank of parameters, unlike Muon, giving Muon a richer associative memory and better performance on tail classes. However, top targeted variants fall the most, and their zero-initialized output projections never gain much rank at all. This implies that the rich learning is a direct consequence of participation by the small singular values.

The parameter effective rank depends on the part of the update that changes the spectrum, meaning the part aligned with the parameter’s own singular basis, and how concentrated it is in the leading directions of this basis. Figure 5 (b) shows this directly: the top targeted and AdamW curves peak at the leading directions, while Muon and the bottom arm stay near uniform. Intuitively, an update that keeps pushing along the leading singular directions of a matrix reinforces what is already there, while a full-spectrum update mostly rotates the basis and leaves the spectrum unchanged. Figure 5 (c) plots these against the final loss. Figure 5 (a) shows the same thing with the isospectral tangent metric of Section 3.3 . Every optimizer puts more of its update into the parameter’s own basis than a random update would, and tangent alignment rises for every optimizer over training, fastest during the cooldown. Among the targeted variants of Muon, the bottom targeted versions show higher alignment than Muon, while the top targeted versions show lower alignment. This is reversed compared to the CIFAR experiments, but it reveals the same underlying phenomenon. In the NanoGPT domain, the targeted region has its magnitude raised, while the remaining regions are relatively suppressed. Therefore, it is simply the top few directions of the gradient which lie within the existing basis of the parameter, and the more you shrink them in the update, the less poorly conditioned the parameter matrices become. Note that structure and performance don’t move together: AdamW collapses rank and still performs well, the bottom targeted variants keep Muon’s rank without matching its loss, and full-spectrum updates keep the spectrum flat for free. still performs well, the bottom targeted variants keep Muon’s rank without matching its loss, and full-spectrum updates keep the spectrum flat for free. This suggests that keeping the spectrum flat is cheap, but isn’t what drives performance.

Our work also suggests an explanation as to why warmup costs Muon but helps AdamW, using the structural plots. AdamW is slow to build structure: its zero-initialized output projections take the whole run to build rank and are still rising at the end (Figure 4 (d)), its early updates lie almost entirely in the parameters’ own frame (Figure 5 (a)), and its gradients have the lowest effective rank of any optimizer over the first hundred steps, lower than any Muon variant that builds structure at all. An elementwise normalized update builds a matrix one bounded increment at a time, so how well it builds depends on how big the first steps are, and with warmup AdamW ends with higher parameter rank and lower loss. An orthogonalized update writes a full-rank matrix in a single step, so Muon’s structure is the same with or without warmup and warmup only throws away full-rate steps.
