2610.31897:364286845f3477bf21aa51c251af2.question: For language models trained with S-SALAAD, what are the measured validation quality, compression ratio, inference memory and latency versus dense training and sparse-plus-low-rank baselines at matched model size and training budget? How much benefit comes from the low-rank component rather than structured sparsity?

passages.text: Scaling laws continue to reward increases in model scale, while the resulting computational and memory demands drive greater reliance on cloud infrastructure for inference. Yet unreliable network connectivity, communication delays, and privacy requirements can make such reliance impractical, motivating local execution on edge devices. Local deployment requires models to fit within limited memory and execute efficiently with the available computational resources. Recent work has shown that learning sparse-plus-low-rank representations enables elastic compression of a single checkpoint to multiple memory budgets. However, fewer parameters do not necessarily translate into faster inference. Indexing overhead and irregular memory access in unstructured sparse components can offset computational savings. To address this critical deployment barrier, we introduce S-SALAAD, a unified framework that jointly learns the model weights and their low-rank and structured sparse components during training. The framework supports a family of hardware-compatible structured sparsity patterns. It couples this structure learning with budget-aware compression and dedicated CPU and GPU kernels that exploit the learned structure for acceleration, enabling efficient inference from a single checkpoint across memory budgets. Experiments on Llama2 and Qwen3 models, covering both pretraining and distillation, show that S-SALAAD advances the empirical Pareto frontier in perplexity, memory, and inference latency across multiple hardware platforms relative to the evaluated baselines. These results show that structured learning can translate elastic compressibility into reduced memory requirements and lower inference latency, enabling practical deployment of large models on edge devices.

Scaling laws ( Kaplan et al., 2020 ) motivate larger models for improved quality, while their memory and computational demands increase reliance on cloud infrastructure with high-end accelerators. However, network connectivity can be unstable in underwater and rescue operations ( Stojanovic & Preisig, 2009 ; Deng et al., 2013 ; Gunn & Anderson, 2015 ) . Safety-critical applications such as autonomous driving require on-device decisions to avoid cloud communication delays ( Liu et al., 2019 ; Kuutti et al., 2021 ; Ma et al., 2025 ; Bodmer et al., 2026 ) , while privacy requirements can prevent sensitive data from being uploaded ( European Parliament and Council of the European Union, 2016 ; Shi et al., 2016 ) . These constraints require large-model inference to move from the cloud to resource-constrained edge devices. Fitting large models within limited memory and achieving low inference latency with the available computational resources are the two critical challenges of this transition. The latency requirement is particularly important in feedback control, where inference latency adds to loop delay and excessive delays can degrade closed-loop performance or destabilize the system, compromising safety ( Shin & Cui, 1995 ; Findeisen & Allgöwer, 2004 ; Ma et al., 2026b ; Ma et al., 2023 ; Nan et al., 2026 ) .

To address memory constraints, existing compression methods use quantization ( Dettmers et al., 2022 ) , distillation ( Gu et al., 2024 ) , pruning ( Sun et al., 2024 ; Frantar & Alistarh, 2023 ; Ashkboos et al., 2024 ) , and low-rank factorization ( Hsu et al., 2022 ; Wang et al., 2025c ) . Varying memory budgets across edge devices call for elastic compression of a single trained checkpoint to multiple model sizes. SALAAD ( Ma et al., 2026a ) enables such elastic compression by learning sparse-and-low-rank (SLR) representations for each linear projection 1 1 1 Here, linear projection refers to a learned linear map in the attention (query/key/value/output) or multi-layer perceptron (MLP; up/gate/down) modules. Embeddings and the language model head are excluded unless noted. during pretraining. However, fewer parameters do not necessarily translate into lower inference latency. Unstructured SLR saves static memory but incurs higher inference latency (see Appendix A.1 ). We identify the overhead from irregular memory access in unstructured sparse operations as a critical barrier to deploying large models on edge devices. Hardware-friendly patterns, including block sparsity ( Okanovic et al., 2025 ) , N : M N\!:\!M sparsity ( Zhao et al., 2024 ) , and row-/column-wise sparsity ( Wen et al., 2016 ) , are therefore required to translate these memory savings into efficient edge inference. A straightforward extension of SALAAD is to impose these patterns on its learned sparse components after pretraining. However, our experiments show that this post-hoc conversion can sharply degrade model performance (see Appendix A.2 ). We therefore induce structured sparsity during pretraining , allowing the SLR components to adapt jointly to the structural constraints.

To this end, we introduce S-SALAAD ( S tructured- S parse- A nd- L ow-Rank A daptation via AD MM), a plug-and-play framework that learns structured SLR representations during pretraining for elastic compression and efficient edge inference. Based on the alternating direction method of multipliers (ADMM), it induces block, N : M N\!:\!M , and row-/column-wise sparsity without changing the model architecture or optimizer update rules. Efficient low-rank updates reduce pretraining overhead, while budget-aware refinement enables zero-shot compression of a single checkpoint to multiple parameter budgets without calibration data or further training. Among these patterns, we identify block sparsity as a practical choice for elastic deployment given current technical capabilities. With dedicated CPU and GPU kernels, the resulting models advance the perplexity–memory–latency Pareto frontier relative to the evaluated baselines. Our contributions are summarized as follows: ❖ A plug-and-play framework for structured-sparsity learning. S-SALAAD jointly learns model weights and their low-rank and structured sparse components under the task loss, adapting the representation to structural constraints during pretraining. S-SALAAD induces block, N : M N\!:\!M , and row-/column-wise sparsity without changing the model architecture, and it is compatible with existing optimizers.

❖ A practical end-to-end implementation. To support the training of larger models and their edge deployment, we address bottlenecks in the training, compression, and inference stages. Specifically, we use i) a warm-started iterative singular value decomposition (I-SVD) to reduce the computational overhead of low-rank updates during pretraining ii) energy-guided alternating refinement (EGAR) to enable zero-shot compression without calibration data or further training, allocating the parameter budget across projections without a preset sparse–low-rank split and reducing reconstruction error within the allocated capacities iii) dedicated CPU and GPU kernels to exploit the induced structured sparsity and reduce inference latency . ❖ Empirical Pareto frontier across training settings. S-SALAAD advances the empirical perplexity–memory–latency Pareto frontier across hardware platforms relative to the evaluated baselines, with each checkpoint supporting multiple compression budgets. These gains hold for Llama2-1B pretraining and cross-architecture distillation from Nemotron-3-Super-120B to Qwen3-1.7B. ❖ Analysis of structured representations. S-SALAAD provides an explicit structured representation of Transformer weights, enabling us to identify distinct sparsity characteristics across linear projection types. Our analysis identifies block sparsity as a practical choice for advancing the perplexity-memory-latency Pareto frontier, combining flexible compression with efficient execution on CPUs and GPUs. Furthermore, we also reveal the relationship between tolerable block granularity and model scale, providing empirical guidance for selecting block sizes when extending S-SALAAD to larger models.

passages.section: A.1 Memory Savings Do Not Guarantee Lower Inference Latency
passages.text: We compare dense inference with the unstructured SLR representation used by SALAAD on a synthetic Llama-1B MLP down projection of size × 5632 2048\!\times\!5632 . The benchmark uses a 15 % 15\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} rank ratio and 5 % 5\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} nonzero density, with the sparse component stored as a PyTorch torch.sparse_csr_tensor . Both representations are profiled on a Quadro RTX 6000 with batch size 128 and sequence length 256. As shown in Figure 7 , static weight memory falls from 23.07 MB 23.07\text{\,}\mathrm{MB} to 10.49 MB 10.49\text{\,}\mathrm{MB} , a 54.5 % 54.5\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} reduction, while throughput falls to 2.68 % 2.68\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} of the dense reference. For this fixed workload, the throughput ratio implies a projection inference latency 37.3 37.3 times that of the dense baseline. Unstructured sparse components incur indexing and irregular memory-access overheads that can offset the computational savings from sparsity ( Mishra et al., 2021 ) . This example illustrates why reduced weight storage alone does not ensure efficient inference. The benchmark uses a synthetic Llama-1B MLP down projection with a 15 % 15\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} rank ratio and 5 % 5\text{\,}\mathrm{\%} nonzero density.

2610.23343:3b49f979f2d33b6e0d83963bdd149.question: For the factorized LoRA objective with weight decay, what rank guarantees are proved, under which assumptions, and what language-model fine-tuning experiments test whether the predicted bottleneck ranks suffice versus standard LoRA?

passages.text: Low-rank adaptation (LoRA) has become the standard method for parameter-efficient fine-tuning of large pretrained models, yet theoretical explanations for why low-rank updates suffice remain incomplete. Most existing analyses rely on the Neural Tangent Kernel (NTK) regime, which linearizes the network around the pretrained weights. In this work, we take a different approach that requires no linearization: our key observation is that, once the backbone is frozen, the loss sees each adapted weight matrix only through a finite-rank linear map induced by the frozen activations. Trace-norm regularization then forces the optimizer to pick a low-rank matrix among all matrices that produce the same observed output. This yields global minimizers whose ranks are controlled by the rank of this map, which we call the bottleneck rank , rather than the sample size. For multi-head attention, we obtain tighter rank upper bounds by exploiting two additional invariances: row-wise softmax is insensitive to additive row constants in the score matrix, and value updates are observable only after attention weighting and frozen output projection. For the factorized LoRA objective with weight decay, we prove a complementary result on the nonconvex side: after an arbitrarily small generic positive semidefinite perturbation, every first-order stationary point is rank-deficient once the LoRA rank exceeds a threshold determined by the bottleneck rank. Finally, we show that global minimizers of the perturbed objective are near-optimal for the original trace-norm problem, and we provide uniform generalization bounds governed by the spectral structure of the frozen features. 0 0 footnotetext: ⋆ Corresponding author.

Fine-tuning large pretrained models on downstream tasks is effective but expensive: updating all parameters of a billion-scale model requires substantial memory and compute. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) solves this problem by adapting a large pretrained model while updating only a small subset of parameters. Some of the representative approaches include adapter modules ( Houlsby et al., 2019 ) , prefix tuning ( Li and Liang, 2021 ) , prompt tuning, and low-rank adaptation (LoRA, Hu et al. 2022 ). Among these, LoRA stands out as an attractive option because it keeps the pretrained backbone frozen and modifies selected linear maps by adding trainable low-rank updates. More formally, for a weight matrix W 0 ∈ ℝ m × n W_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} , LoRA parameterizes the adapted weight as W = W 0 + T , T = U ​ V ⊤ , U ∈ ℝ m × r , V ∈ ℝ n × r , W=W_{0}+T,\qquad T=UV^{\top},\qquad U\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times r},V\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r}, The rank r r is typically chosen by the practitioner as a hyperparameter rather than something derived from the fine-tuning objective itself ( Hu et al., 2022 ; Schulman and Lab, 2025 ) . A fundamental theoretical question is therefore: When does the regularized fine-tuning objective itself admit a low-rank global minimizer, and what controls the rank?

Most existing theory addresses nearby questions through linearization or simplified training dynamics. In the NTK regime, Jang et al. (2024) shows that full fine-tuning admits a low-rank solution and that sufficiently overparameterized LoRA eliminates spurious local minima. Afzal et al. (2025) analyze fine-tuning through linearization under an explicit ℓ 2 \ell_{2} bias toward the pretrained model. Beyond classical linearization, Kim et al. (2025) study LoRA dynamics and prove a dichotomy between convergence to a low-rank global minimizer and convergence to a qualitatively different high-rank solution. These works are complementary to ours, but they do not answer a more structural question: what property of the objective function makes low-rank optima available in the first place?

• Low-rank representer theorem for trace-norm fine-tuning. For a frozen network in which an adapted block T T is observed only through a finite-rank linear map Φ ⁡ ( T ) \Phi(T) of bottleneck rank d Φ d_{\Phi} , we prove that the trace-norm-regularized problem has a global minimizer whose rank is controlled by d Φ d_{\Phi} ; see Theorem 4.1 . The multi-stage extension is Theorem 4.3 . • Rank bounds from attention invariances. For multi-head attention, query and key updates are observable only through centered score subspaces because row-wise softmax is invariant to row-wise additive constants. Value updates are observable only after attention weighting and frozen output projection. Combining these invariances with projector compression gives the optimizer-dependent subspace rank bounds in Theorem 4.4 . • Generic first-order rank deficiency for factorized LoRA. For the weight-decayed LoRA factorization, we prove that after a generic positive semidefinite perturbation, full-column-rank first-order stationary points are excluded whenever the Pataki–Barvinok rank threshold exceeds the dimension of the associated family of symmetric KKT matrices; see Theorem 4.7 . The multistage and attention consequence are Theorem C.9 and Corollary 4.8 . This is a first-order exclusion theorem, not a no-spurious-local-minima theorem; Proposition 4.9 gives an explicit limitation. • Perturbation transfer and generalization. We show that global minimizers of the perturbed factorized objective are near-optimal for the original trace-norm-regularized problem when the perturbation is small; see Theorem 4.10 .

Fine-tuning large pretrained models on downstream tasks is effective but expensive: updating all parameters of a billion-scale model requires substantial memory and compute. Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) solves this problem by adapting a large pretrained model while updating only a small subset of parameters. Some of the representative approaches include adapter modules ( Houlsby et al., 2019 ) , prefix tuning ( Li and Liang, 2021 ) , prompt tuning, and low-rank adaptation (LoRA, Hu et al. 2022 ). Among these, LoRA stands out as an attractive option because it keeps the pretrained backbone frozen and modifies selected linear maps by adding trainable low-rank updates. More formally, for a weight matrix W 0 ∈ ℝ m × n W_{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n} , LoRA parameterizes the adapted weight as W = W 0 + T , T = U ​ V ⊤ , U ∈ ℝ m × r , V ∈ ℝ n × r , W=W_{0}+T,\qquad T=UV^{\top},\qquad U\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times r},V\in\mathbb{R}^{n\times r}, The rank r r is typically chosen by the practitioner as a hyperparameter rather than something derived from the fine-tuning objective itself ( Hu et al., 2022 ; Schulman and Lab, 2025 ) . A fundamental theoretical question is therefore: When does the regularized fine-tuning objective itself admit a low-rank global minimizer, and what controls the rank?

Most existing theory addresses nearby questions through linearization or simplified training dynamics. In the NTK regime, Jang et al. (2024) shows that full fine-tuning admits a low-rank solution and that sufficiently overparameterized LoRA eliminates spurious local minima. Afzal et al. (2025) analyze fine-tuning through linearization under an explicit ℓ 2 \ell_{2} bias toward the pretrained model. Beyond classical linearization, Kim et al. (2025) study LoRA dynamics and prove a dichotomy between convergence to a low-rank global minimizer and convergence to a qualitatively different high-rank solution. These works are complementary to ours, but they do not answer a more structural question: what property of the objective function makes low-rank optima available in the first place?

2611.07859:fb745695e6daaf6a956bba51ec895.question: In the controlled closed-search evaluations, how does CORE compare with the Tongyi DeepResearch and OpenResearcher harnesses on answer accuracy, evidence recall, context length, and cost? Which ablations isolate snippet selection, context expansion, and duplicate suppression?

passages.text: Deep research agents answer complex questions through repeated search. They rely on a harness that runs their tool calls and returns evidence to their context. This creates a trade-off: Search works best over long passages, which give enough context for reliable semantic matching. But the returned evidence should be short, because every observation stays in the agent’s context for the rest of the trajectory. We introduce CORE , a training-free harness that combines coarse-to-fine search with context management. CORE retrieves passages with a dense retriever. It then reuses the token-level similarities from a late-interaction reranker to return only the most relevant snippet from each passage. Context management lets the agent expand the context around sources it has already retrieved and suppresses repeated snippets. In controlled closed-search comparisons with the Tongyi DeepResearch and OpenResearcher harnesses, CORE achieves state-of-the-art answer accuracy and evidence recall across three agent models and three benchmarks (BrowseComp-Plus, BrowseComp-Wikipedia and BrowseComp-Plus CM ), on corpora containing up to 553M documents.

The key idea of our CORE, a co arse-to-fine deep re search harness, is to shift this burden from the agent to the search itself: relevant text is found by searching over broad passages, while the agent receives only concise snippets. We organize the search space into documents, passages, segments, and snippets, and treat evidence as the text admitted into the agent’s context to serve the local goal of a sub-query or the global goal of the question. CORE’s search tool first performs coarse retrieval of passages with a reasoning-aware dense retriever ( Chen et al., 2026b ) , then fine-grained reranking with a late-interaction model ( Khattab and Zaharia, 2020 ; Chaffin, 2025 ) , whose token-level similarities also locate the most relevant snippet within each passage at no additional encoding cost. CORE’s context manager lets the agent expand the context around previously retrieved sources and deduplicates snippets across searches. Our contributions are as follows: • Coarse-to-fine search. CORE searches at the passage level but returns evidence at the snippet level. It reuses the token-level similarities computed during late-interaction reranking to locate the most relevant snippet in each passage, without any additional encoding. • A training-free harness. CORE combines coarse-to-fine search with context management and works with any agent model without retraining. Context management offsets the narrowness of snippet-level evidence by letting the agent expand the context around previously retrieved sources, and it suppresses snippets repeated across searches.

• State-of-the-art closed-search results at scale. Under controlled settings, we compare CORE with two recent state-of-the-art open-source harnesses, Tongyi DeepResearch ( Tongyi DeepResearch Team et al., 2025 ) and OpenResearcher ( Li et al., 2026b ) , on BrowseComp-Plus ( Chen et al., 2026c ) , BrowseComp-Wikipedia ( Yang et al., 2026 ) , and BrowseComp-Plus CM ( Sharifymoghaddam et al., 2026 ) . To ensure reproducibility, we restrict the study to closed search over fixed corpora. Across three agent models, CORE achieves the highest accuracy and evidence recall in every model–benchmark comparison, setting new state-of-the-art results to the best of our knowledge.

Table 1: Main comparison results. Answer accuracy and evidence recall are in percent. Peak context is the median, over questions, of the maximum context length in tokens. Tokens/search is the mean number of tokens returned per search call, summed over all subqueries. Search calls is the mean number of search calls per question. Token counts are comparable only within the same agent model. Arrows show the preferred direction, and bold marks the best value in each of these columns within each model–benchmark group. We find that Tongyi-DeepResearch-30B-A3B, using the original Tongyi DeepResearch harness with document-level retrieval based on AgentIR-4B, achieves 63.13% on BrowseComp-Plus, which is lower than the 65.66% achieved by our current passage-level retrieval setup. On BrowseComp-Plus, Jiang et al. (2026) report an evidence recall of 38.1% for Tongyi-DeepResearch-30B-A3B, whereas their Harness-1 (20B) reported the evidence recall at 58.4%.

We presented CORE , a training-free deep research harness that combines coarse-to-fine search with context management. CORE retrieves whole passages to judge relevance, then reuses the reranker’s token-level similarities to return only the most relevant snippet from each one. Context management lets the agent expand the context around sources it has already retrieved and suppresses repeated snippets. Across three agent models and three benchmarks, CORE achieves higher answer accuracy and evidence recall than Tongyi DeepResearch and OpenResearcher in every model–benchmark comparison, while returning substantially fewer tokens per search than Tongyi DeepResearch. These results show that deep research agents can answer more accurately from shorter search responses when relevant text is selected before it enters their context.

Sampling parameters follow Appendix A.2 ; context budgets and tool-call formats follow each model’s configuration. 2610.20857:437ff6d424bf6e6bdc4657a4e9414.question: How does IDEA2PRIOR evaluate paper-retrieval quality against its baselines, including query selection, relevance judgments, Hit@5 accounting, and retrieval cost? Which components are usable in a handwritten research-digest harness?

passages.text: Finding a paper from an informal research idea requires more than matching topic words: relevant work may use different terminology, and its distinguishing mechanism may be absent from the abstract. We present Idea2Prior, an auditable literature-search system built on PaperArena. It combines multi-source discovery, identity verification, facet-based abstract assessment, semantic citation expansion, and joint Expert ranking. A retrieval-only mode ranks up to five papers from a shortlist of at most 60, using complete available abstracts and locally selected PDF evidence from five fixed acquisition attempts, without generating a long-form report. In a historical comparison covering ten queries from each of EASY, MEDIUM, and HARD, aggregate reported Hit@5 is 53.3% for Idea2Prior, 43.3% for ChatGPT web Deep Research, and 36.7% for Gemini web Deep Research under the documented accounting convention. The advantage is concentrated in EASY and MEDIUM; ChatGPT leads on HARD. Selected Idea2Prior runs average 8 minutes 53 seconds, compared with user-reported web averages of 5.2 and 4.7 minutes. A separate nine-query API sample averages $0.0945 per task; this is a historical cost observation, not a matched comparison with web subscription costs. Pairwise Top 5 coverage ranges from 6% to 34%, showing differing returned evidence sets. The system also exposes optional implementation analysis and citation-evolution tools. These results support targeted idea-to-paper retrieval while leaving general web research, forum search, and broader relevance evaluation open.

Researchers often remember an idea before they remember a title: a neighborhood with uncertain boundaries, a circuit transformation with a particular constraint, or an assistant that recognizes when a complex task changes. Recovering relevant prior work from such descriptions is difficult because vocabulary, application setting, and the level of technical detail can differ substantially between a query and a paper. A useful assistant must retrieve candidates, establish their bibliographic identities, and distinguish a close conceptual match from work that merely shares a topic. LLM-based research systems provide useful ways to explore and synthesize sources. STORM organizes research into multi-perspective information gathering and article outlining [ 3 ] , Co-STORM supports interactive exploration [ 4 ] , and Agent Laboratory connects literature review with experimentation and reporting [ 5 ] . Our focus is narrower: given an idea, which five identifiable papers are most likely to match it, and what evidence explains their selection? This objective is not equivalent to the quality of a general research report. We introduce Idea2Prior, an extension of PaperArena and its implementation [ 1 , 2 ] . The contribution is an engineering and evaluation framework for inspectable idea-to-paper retrieval: it preserves search queries, candidate identities, assessments, filtering reasons, PDF availability, and the final ranking. This makes it possible to distinguish a discovery miss from a candidate that was retrieved but lost during filtering, or from a task that failed operationally. A high-level result alone cannot make those distinctions.

The central design separates inexpensive assessment of a broad candidate pool from a bounded examination of document evidence. After abstract assessment and citation expansion, an Expert model jointly considers up to 60 candidates. Five papers are selected for PDF acquisition; unavailable PDFs are not replaced by additional papers in retrieval-only mode. Complete available abstracts remain in the Expert input, along with evidence availability and up to six locally selected PDF passages per acquired paper. A missing PDF does not make a paper irrelevant and does not prevent it from ranking first. The optional full-report mode retains downstream synthesis for users who need a written literature analysis. The revised evaluation covers 30 query cases: ten from each of three prompt tiers, with shared targets across tiers. The reported aggregate Hit@5 is 16/30 for Idea2Prior, 13/30 for ChatGPT web Deep Research, and 11/30 for Gemini web Deep Research. The ChatGPT total includes one convention-based credit, disclosed in Section 5.1 . Idea2Prior leads both baselines by 20 percentage points on EASY and MEDIUM, but trails ChatGPT by 10 points on HARD. Mean selected-run latency is 8.89 minutes, and a separately reported nine-query cost sample averages $0.0945. Thus the present evidence shows a recovery advantage in two tiers and a low observed API cost, with longer latency than the supplied browser averages. Our contributions are: 1. An auditable retrieval-and-ranking workflow with identity-aware candidate records, semantic citation filtering, and a joint Top 5 decision over a bounded shortlist.

2. A retrieval-only execution mode that preserves abstract and PDF evidence assessment while omitting report-specific processing, exposed through local web, Python, CLI, and Notebook interfaces. 3. A three-system historical evaluation with explicit target-recovery, agreement, latency, token, and cost accounting, together with preserved prompts and outputs. 4. Optional implementation-analysis, citation-evolution, planning, benchmark-landscape, and citation-gap extensions, with their earlier exploratory evaluations distinguished from the retrieval benchmark.

Our comparison addresses finding papers from research ideas. It does not evaluate general website exploration, forum search, comprehensive web research, report quality, legal patent novelty, or the correctness of every citation recommendation. General web and forum capabilities remain limited. A designated-target miss can coexist with useful related papers, so target Hit@5 should be complemented by independently adjudicated relevance and usefulness.

Idea2Prior extends PaperArena with an auditable workflow for retrieving and ranking papers from research ideas. Joint ranking combines an abstract-level shortlist with bounded, explicitly partial PDF evidence, while a retrieval-only mode avoids report-specific work. In the documented historical comparison, aggregate reported Hit@5 is 53.3%, exceeding the two browser baselines overall, with a clear HARD-tier exception and longer reported latency. A separate historical cost sample averages $0.0945 per query. These findings motivate focused scholarly retrieval with inspectable evidence; they do not establish general Deep Research superiority, calibrated novelty assessment, or a matched baseline cost advantage.

2611.06598:8aa176c45890621d9499e70a48ea4.question: In the LoRA fine-tuning experiments, how is behavioral compression rate measured, which adapter-compression baselines and held-out behavior tests are used, and how well do correction spectra predict rate across base models and noisy datasets?

passages.text: Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA) adapts a frozen language model through a compact learned update, making it a natural setting for asking how much information fine-tuning needs to write. Yet adapter rank, parameter count, or numerical reconstruction error do not directly tell us how many bits are required to preserve the acquired behavior. We therefore define an operational behavioral rate R ⋆ R^{\star} as the smallest serialized size of a compressed adapter that, once reloaded into the frozen base model, retains a fixed fraction of its held-out fine-tuning gain. Across LoRA fine-tuning experiments, this rate increases with distinct training content at fixed optimization budgets, but is not determined by intuitive metrics like source description length, fine-tuning gain, or weight-space reconstruction error. Most importantly, the same datasets exhibit substantially different, and even reordered, rates across frozen base models, showing that fine-tuning compressibility is a property of the dataset–receiver pair rather than of the dataset alone. However, we show that correction spectra measured on the data are able to rank these rates within a receiver. Finally, we study a striking noise-reducing effect of compression: adapters trained on deliberately corrupted datasets fall far below the frozen model, yet after compression score above it (23.7% to 82.9% on GSM8K, against 77.6% for frozen Qwen2.5-7B), consistently across tested families and sizes.
